name: Griffith's Criterion
statement: A crack in a brittle solid propagates catastrophically once its length exceeds a critical value set by the balance of released strain energy and new surface energy.
statementAccent: balance of released strain energy and new surface energy
meaning: Griffith's criterion explains why real brittle materials fail far below their theoretical bond strength: pre-existing flaws concentrate stress. Fracture occurs when the elastic strain energy released by extending a crack exceeds the energy needed to create the two new fracture surfaces. This yields a critical condition in which fracture stress times the square root of crack length equals a constant set by the elastic modulus and surface energy.
mechanism: Griffith treated fracture as a thermodynamic energy balance. As a crack grows, stored elastic strain energy is released, while creating new surface costs energy proportional to the surface energy. The system's free energy peaks at a critical crack length; beyond that point further growth lowers total energy, so the crack runs unstably.

examples.text: Bulk glass fractures near 100 MPa though its atomic bond strength is about 10,000 MPa; Griffith showed microscopic flaws account for the gap.
The criterion accurately predicts fracture in brittle materials like glass and ceramics, where plastic deformation at the crack tip is minimal.
Irwin and Orowan (around 1948–1949) added a plastic-dissipation term so the energy balance could apply to ductile metals such as steel.

whyItMatters: It founded fracture mechanics by showing that flaw size, not just applied stress, governs failure. This reframed strength as a defect-controlled property and led directly to modern damage-tolerant design and the stress-intensity approach.
limits: The original criterion applies to ideally brittle materials; for ductile metals the required surface-energy values are unrealistically low, because most energy goes into crack-tip plastic deformation. It assumes linear-elastic behavior and pre-existing sharp flaws, and Irwin and Orowan's plastic-work term was needed to extend it to ductile solids.
misreadings: It does not say materials fracture at their theoretical atomic strength; the whole point is that flaws make them far weaker. Nor does it directly apply to ductile fracture without the plastic-energy correction.
origin: Alan Arnold Griffith, "The phenomena of rupture and flow in solids," Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 1921.

sources.text: Wikipedia's article on fracture mechanics, giving Griffith's 1921 paper, the energy-balance criterion, the glass strength paradox, and the Irwin-Orowan plastic-term modification — supports the statement, mechanism, and limits.

Wikipedia's article on fracture, confirming fracture strength was first theoretically estimated by Alan Arnold Griffith in 1921, relating it to Young's modulus, surface energy, and micro-crack length — supports the attribution.
